image_description: A close-up, eye-level shot of a turtle resting on rocky ground. The turtle has a dark, high-domed carapace with visible scute patterns and some yellowish markings. Its head is extended, showing a pointed snout and small lateral eyes. The skin on the neck and limbs appears rough and textured. The front limbs are visible, appearing stout with claws. The background is blurred, suggesting shallow depth of field.

checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The head is clearly visible, proportionally large relative to the shell opening, with a distinct pointed snout and small eye on the side of the head.

checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The shell exhibits a high dome and oval shape. The color is dark brown/black with lighter markings. The surface appears smooth with some glossiness, consistent with the description.

checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: While there are ridges along the scute sutures, distinct 'longitudinal keels' (three separate raised ridges running down the length) are not clearly defined as prominent features; the shell looks more uniformly domed or the keels are very subtle/worn, which might indicate an adult or a different species variant, but strictly speaking, the specific 'three keels' feature is not distinctly visible as described for juveniles.

checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The plastron (underside) is completely occluded by the turtle's body and the angle of the photo. It cannot be verified.

checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible skin on the neck and legs is dark grey/brown and shows a distinct rough, tuberculate/scaly texture.

The tail is not visible in this frame; it is occluded by the rear of the shell and the angle.

The toes on the front left foot appear to merge slightly into the rock surface. The definition of individual toes and claws is somewhat muddy and lacks crisp edges, suggesting slight generation blur or fusion with the ground.
The eye reflection and the curve of the snout have a slight unnatural warping, common in AI generations where spherical objects meet complex textures.

To verify that the turtle sits correctly on the rocks with appropriate contact shadows and depth separation, ensuring no floating elements.
